jsnvu6-e178375-d1e103.summary: Rubric announcing the general and special exposition (sententia) of Book 3, Distinction 23.

jsnvu6-e178375-d1e110.summary: General division of the text: Lombard turns from the mysteries of the incarnate Word, by which we are restored to God effectively, to the virtues and gifts by which we are led back to God formally. The section on the gratuitous habits is divided into the habits themselves (theological, then cardinal virtues from d.33) and their interconnection (d.36), before the precepts (d.37). Within the theological virtues, faith is treated in itself (d.23), in relation to its object (d.24), and in relation to believers (d.25); d.23 itself first gives a formal account of faith—definition, explanation, and an incidental doubt—and then its material object, the non-apparent.
claims: The treatment of virtues concerns how we are reduced to God formally, as the preceding christological material concerned how we are reduced effectively
Lombard's treatment of faith is divided into faith in itself (d.23), in relation to its object (d.24), and in relation to believers (d.25)
concepts: formal vs. effective return to God

jsnvu6-e178375-d1e182.summary: Special exposition of Lombard's d.23: whether Christ had faith and hope as he had charity; the definition of faith as the virtue by which one believes what is not seen; faith as habit in the mind versus faith as the creed believed; the distinction of unformed and formed faith, only the latter being virtue; the triple distinction credere Deum, credere Deo, credere in Deum, the last proper to the good; whether unformed faith remains and becomes formed when charity arrives (Lombard inclines to yes); the unity of faith in object and in species; faith as concerning the non-apparent, with the Pauline definition 'substance of things hoped for, argument of things not apparent' (Heb. 11); and whether that description also fits hope.
claims: Faith as a virtue is a habit in the mind, distinct from the articles believed
Only formed faith, working through love, is a virtue in the full sense
Credere in Deum, unlike credere Deum and credere Deo, belongs only to those with formed faith
Lombard prefers to say that unformed faith remains and is made formed by the arrival of charity
Faith is one in the believed object and one in species, not number, across believers

jsnvu6-e178375.summary: Praeambulum to Book 3, Distinction 23: a divisio textus and expositio of Peter Lombard's text on faith. In general, it places d.23 within Lombard's larger plan—after the mysteries by which we are restored to God effectively come the virtues by which we return formally—subdividing the virtues into theological and cardinal, and faith into faith in itself (d.23), in relation to its object (d.24), and in relation to believers (d.25). In particular, it paraphrases Lombard's account: whether Christ had faith and hope, the definition of faith as the virtue by which one believes what is not seen, faith as habit versus faith as creed, formed versus unformed faith, the triad credere Deum/Deo/in Deum, whether unformed faith becomes formed, the specific unity of faith, and the Pauline definition of Hebrews 11.
claims: Distinction 23 treats faith in itself, preparing for faith's object (d.24) and its believers (d.25)
Only faith formed by charity is a virtue properly speaking, though unformed faith is a gift of God
